task-intent.statement: The epic's closing dispatch, sent under the role name every delegated Commander in this epic had already been dispatched under.

expected-behavior.statement: The role tier table merged one wave earlier would resolve a model for it, since the table was proved against a live crew before merge.

observed-behavior.statement: The dispatch was refused by that table: no model tier declared for role 'commander-delegated' under harness 'claude' -- refusing rather than guessing. Live doctrine names 7 role terms (reviewer 84, commander 74, implementer 42, critic 29, admiral 22, cartographer 8, commander-delegated 7) and the table declared the first six. The omitted key was the one 10 registry entries in this epic used.

impact-cost.statement: One full gate cycle: a lane opened, worktreed, dispatched, gated and merged solely to declare one key and guard its provenance. The epic's own deliverable blocked the epic.

workaround.statement: None taken at the refusal point. The lane declared the key at the human's ruled tier and added a guard that scans doctrine for the property the table depends on.

diagnosis.statement: The refusal is the design working -- failing closed on an undeclared role rather than guessing a tier, pinned by tests/test_crew_launcher.py:1123. What was wrong was the provenance of the key set: it enumerated the roles its author expected the corpus to use, and the proof-of-life covered one key rather than the set.

task-intent.statement: Clearing a blocked dispatch when the blocker was a one-line table entry and the Admiral held the keyboard.

expected-behavior.statement: A one-line fix is small enough to be integration work rather than delegated work.

observed-behavior.statement: Two shortcuts were available and both were declined. Patching the key directly would have skipped the guard, which was the larger half of the value. Relabeling the blocked commander dispatch as 'implementer' would have passed the tier check by writing a false role onto a 10-gate commander spine, and would have fed the same wave's role-spine drift lint a lie.

impact-cost.statement: One gate cycle spent instead of one line typed. The deadlock -- no commander-delegated crew can be dispatched until the table is fixed -- actively argued for the shortcut.

workaround.statement: Serialized two lanes: an implementer declares the key and writes the guard, and the blocked commander dispatch waits until the declaration is legal rather than until the label is convenient.

task-intent.statement: Retiring skills/workbench entirely, on the reading that its teaching had been cut to a 20-line stub and the package was dead weight.

expected-behavior.statement: A move plus a text update: the launch order was written from a live-referrer census of the repo tree, which showed a stub plus templates.

observed-behavior.statement: The human called a corpus reinstall before the lane launched, and the reinstall showed the deletion target does not exist as described. install_constellation.py:229 bundles checklist_engine.py and gauge_writer_hook.py under workbench; :848-849 hard-code HOOK_OWNER_SKILL = 'workbench'; :929 points the installed hook path at constellation-workbench/scripts/. The installed package carries 7 engine scripts and ~/.claude/settings.json wires 5 hook entries plus 1 permission rule there, including the spine_rail.py Stop hook enforcing this very run.

impact-cost.statement: The order as written would have shipped a deletion that unwired the Stop hook, the SessionStart hook, the gauge writer and the engine path on every installed machine. It was caught by the human's sequencing, not by the Admiral's census.

workaround.statement: The lane was closed unsent and its order kept unlaunched. The teaching issue closed on what actually shipped; the package coupling was filed separately to be done deliberately with its own settings.json migration path.

diagnosis.statement: The installer only knows how to ship skills -- :322-324 raises InstallError for any skills/* directory without a parseable SKILL.md -- so a script bundle must wear a SKILL.md to be installable at all. The skill is vestigial and the wrapper is load-bearing, which a census of the repo tree cannot distinguish because the coupling lives in the installer's constants rather than in any reference to the files.

task-intent.statement: Counting live referrers to six workbench files, to tell the human what was genuinely deletable at the cheap tier.

expected-behavior.statement: Excluding .agent-work/ from the search cuts archived run artifacts, which quote paths as history rather than depending on them.

observed-behavior.statement: That exclusion also dropped .agent-work/templates/TEMPLATES_MANIFEST.json, a tracked overlay manifest that is a live referrer. One file was reported as having zero referrers when it has two, and re-measuring showed all six files have live referrers -- checklist-engine.md 32, status-model.md 10, STATE_NOTE 9, WORKFLOW_CLOSEOUT 8, CONSTELLATION_FEEDBACK 5, DEFAULT 2. This was the third bad count of the same file set in two days.

impact-cost.statement: It changed the answer rather than a detail of it: there was no deletion available at the cheap tier at all, which is what closed the lane.

workaround.statement: Corrected to the human before the number was acted on. The earlier bad counts were caught by implausibility (125 and 180 referrers) rather than by measuring correctly, which is a weaker check.

diagnosis.statement: A path-shaped exclusion filter cannot separate archive noise from tracked content when both live under the same prefix, and .agent-work/ holds both an archive and a tracked template overlay.

task-intent.statement: Dispatching an implementer with a spine, so it would drive its plan through the MCP door like every other lane in this epic.

expected-behavior.statement: Every role in this corpus has a spine, so init_work_area.py --role implementer would provision one.

observed-behavior.statement: No implementer spine role exists. The provisioning call rejected the argument and the --spine form wanted a path that had nothing to point at. The lane was dispatched with --handoff/--result and no SPINE_FILE, so its door bound nothing, and it drove its own IMPLEMENTER_PLAN.json through scripts/checklist_engine.py instead.

impact-cost.statement: The Admiral's own dispatch shape forced a CLI use inside the epic whose subject is removing the CLI as an agent-facing path. Two failed provisioning commands before the shape was understood.

workaround.statement: Dispatched on the result-artifact shape, which is the correct shape for a role judged on a deliverable rather than a terminal state.

diagnosis.statement: The door binds one spine at process start, so a role with no spine is a role the door structurally cannot serve. This sits in the same family as the self-waive refusal and the archive-move deadlock -- the door's path, identity and spine are all fixed before the work starts -- and is the sharpest instance, because it is not a run acting on itself but a role with nothing to bind.

task-intent.statement: Reinstalling the corpus onto the human's machine so the wave-3 deliverables would be live rather than inert.

expected-behavior.statement: The installer-writes-into-the-calling-repo defect was fixed and closed one wave earlier, so a self-install should leave the tracked tree clean.

observed-behavior.statement: The install rewrote the tracked .mcp.json, replacing python3 with a probed machine-local py. It happened on this session's install and on the previous session's, and was reverted both times.

impact-cost.statement: A tracked file dirtied on every self-install, carrying an interpreter name that is correct only on the machine that ran the installer.

workaround.statement: git checkout -- .mcp.json after each install. Recorded rather than reopened, under the standing ruling against minting new tracking mid-epic.

diagnosis.statement: The closed fix stopped the installer targeting the wrong checkout. It did not stop it writing a machine-local interpreter into a tracked file when the target checkout is the right one, which is the remaining half.

task-intent.statement: Authoring the wave-4 replan transition packet that closes the epic's last wave boundary with decision=stop.

expected-behavior.statement: Copying the previous boundary's INPUT and updating it would produce a valid packet, since the templates are the same two files at every boundary.

observed-behavior.statement: The verifier refused six times in sequence, each on a different rule: completed_outcomes entries must be objects; completed and open ids must exactly partition the current-wave issue ids, twice; result.current_wave.issues must be nonempty even when the decision is to stop; a discrepancy classification forces a specific disposition action; material_changes entries must be objects. The two partition failures came from copying the previous INPUT, whose current_plan.current_wave still held the wave before it.

impact-cost.statement: Six verifier round-trips to author one packet, all at the boundary where the epic had nothing left to launch.

workaround.statement: Chain the previous boundary's RESULT current_wave into the next boundary's INPUT current_plan.current_wave, rather than carrying the previous INPUT forward. The verifier enforces this and neither template states it.

task-intent.statement: Shipping a bookend freeze and a drift lint that stop a run deleting the steps that make it finish.

expected-behavior.statement: A merged, green, gated deliverable on main is a delivered deliverable.

observed-behavior.statement: Both were inert on main. The lint named its own gap precisely -- repo=['closeout','init'] installed=[] for the admiral template, and the same shape for commander and explorer -- because the freeze reads declarations from the installed corpus, not the repo source. After the human ordered a reinstall it flipped to all 3 role spine template(s) declare bookends and match the installed corpus.

impact-cost.statement: Between merge and reinstall, two deliverables the epic reported as shipped protected nothing on the machine that runs the agents.

workaround.statement: The reinstall was requested from the human rather than performed unasked, because it is a deployment action on their machine and this session had already reverted one installer-caused change.

diagnosis.statement: For anything the installed corpus reads rather than the repo source, merged and deployed are different states, and the suite can only see the first.

task-intent.statement: Beginning the closeout gate after the last lane merged, with the run's context nearly spent.

expected-behavior.statement: A gate whose remaining work is bounded -- episodes, a summary, acceptance -- can be started at whatever context is left.

observed-behavior.statement: The engine refused the start outright: context at 18% is at/over the hard limit, so this is not the moment to BEGIN work here. It named the exact recovery call with a concrete why_ref rather than a placeholder, logged the refusal to a trip ledger and a permanent trip history, and left the DIGEST as the handoff a fresh agent would read. After the session was compacted the advisory cleared on its own and the same start succeeded.

impact-cost.statement: None to the run. The refusal held the gate closed for one exchange.

workaround.statement: Compaction rather than the refresh handshake, at the human's instruction. The engine reads context from a gauge file the hook rewrites, so a compacted session presents fresh and the same call is permitted.

diagnosis.statement: This is a hard refusal on begin, distinct from the soft-band advisory the Stop hook overrides -- the engine blocks starting new work at low context but never blocks closing the gate already open.
